title: Source Library for Palestine
subtitle: A practical reading map for Islamic sources, history, law, and current reporting
summary: A reliable study of Palestine needs more than a single article. This guide groups useful primary sources, historical scholarship, legal material, and dated reporting so readers can check claims and understand their limits.

sections.title: How to Build a Reliable Reading List
sections.body: No single source answers every question about Palestine. A strong reading list combines Islamic scripture and scholarship with historical documents, academic studies, legal findings, and dated reporting. Each source should be identified by its author, purpose, date, and evidence.

sections.title: Verify Before Repeating a Claim
sections.body:
The Qur'an teaches a principle that applies directly to news and social media:

"O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful." (Qur'an 49:6)

Check the original report, date, location, named sources, and later corrections. When evidence is incomplete, say that it is incomplete. Careful verification is not indifference to suffering; it is part of refusing to harm people through false claims.

sections.title: Islamic Scripture and Scholarship
sections.body:
Begin with the Quran and soundly transmitted Prophetic teachings when asking why Palestine matters to Muslims. The opening of Surah al-Isra describes the Prophet's night journey to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, while Surah al-Hajj names monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques among places whose protection matters. Read these texts with recognized tafsir and responsible scholarship rather than using isolated quotations as political slogans.

For Islamic law and ethics, distinguish Quranic commands, hadith reports, classical legal reasoning, and modern political claims. They are related, but they are not interchangeable.

sections.title: History and Primary Documents
sections.body:
For modern history, use books that explain the late Ottoman period, the British Mandate, the 1948 Nakba, the 1967 occupation, the PLO, and the Intifadas. Pair a historian's interpretation with primary documents such as mandate records, United Nations resolutions, speeches, agreements, maps, and demographic records. A document proves what an institution recorded or said; it still requires context and comparison.

Rashid Khalidi and Beshara Doumani are useful for Palestinian identity and local social history. The United Nations' Palestine portal is useful for locating official documents and timelines. Academic works should be compared where historians disagree.

sections.title: Law, Humanitarian Data, and Current Events
sections.body:
For international-law questions, read the actual judgments, advisory opinions, treaty text, and submissions rather than relying on headlines. For humanitarian conditions, prefer dated datasets and methodology notes from organizations such as the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and UNRWA. For breaking news, use reporting that names sources, distinguishes confirmed facts from allegations, and corrects errors openly.

Legal and humanitarian sources answer specific questions; they do not by themselves settle every theological, historical, or political question. Keeping those categories separate makes the overall argument stronger.

sections.title: A Simple Method for Readers
sections.body:
For any important claim, ask four questions: Who made the claim? What evidence is provided? When was it published or recorded? Can the original material be checked? Then compare at least one source with a different perspective while keeping the evidence, not the label, central.

Avoid anonymous screenshots, undated videos, cropped quotations, and claims that treat all Palestinians, Israelis, Muslims, Jews, or Christians as a single mind. The aim is truthful understanding, protection of human dignity, and moral accountability.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Reading Palestine Responsibly
sections.body: A trustworthy reading process joins faith, evidence, and humility. Read Islamic sources for the moral and religious significance of Palestine, historical scholarship for context, primary documents for what institutions recorded, and current reporting for carefully dated events. Verify before repeating, distinguish fact from interpretation, and keep justice and human dignity at the center.

furtherReading.title: United Nations: Question of Palestine
furtherReading.author: United Nations
furtherReading.note: Official documents, resolutions, reports, and background material. Read each document with attention to its date, author, and institutional mandate.

furtherReading.title: United Nations Timeline of the Question of Palestine
furtherReading.author: United Nations
furtherReading.note: A dated orientation to major developments; use the linked documents for fuller context.

furtherReading.title: Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness
furtherReading.author: Rashid Khalidi
furtherReading.note: A major scholarly study of Palestinian identity and its historical development.

furtherReading.title: Rediscovering Palestine: Merchants and Peasants in Jabal Nablus, 1700–1900
furtherReading.author: Beshara B. Doumani
furtherReading.note: A social and economic history that grounds discussion of Palestine in families, towns, trade, and local institutions.

furtherReading.title: The Israel-Palestine Conflict: A History
furtherReading.author: James L. Gelvin
furtherReading.note: An accessible historical survey that places Palestinian and Israeli national movements in their wider context.

furtherReading.title: Armed Struggle and the Search for State
furtherReading.author: Yezid Sayigh
furtherReading.note: A detailed history of the Palestinian national movement and the PLO.

furtherReading.title: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs: Occupied Palestinian Territory
furtherReading.author: United Nations OCHA
furtherReading.note: Situation reports, maps, and humanitarian data. Check publication dates and methodology for every statistic.

furtherReading.title: UNRWA: Palestine Refugees
furtherReading.author: United Nations Relief and Works Agency
furtherReading.note: Official information about the agency's mandate and services to Palestine refugees; distinguish institutional reporting from independent analysis.
